blurb: How electricity actually gets made (solar cells, wind, hydro, geothermal, gas turbines, coal, fuel cells), compared on cost, capacity factor, dispatchability, and build time.
question: What should generate this electricity?
title: Power Generation: A Practical Reference
lede: The cheapest ways to make electricity are mostly the ones you can't turn on when you want them, and that trade decides most generation projects. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} technologies across seven classes, from silicon solar cells to hydrogen-fired turbines, with the cost, capacity factor, and build-time numbers a project actually buys on.

facets.label: Dispatch
facets.tip: How much control an operator has over output, which is this sheet's organizing axis. Variable = the resource sets output (sun, wind, waves, an unregulated river). Baseload = ramps slowly and is economically must-run once started. Dispatchable = follows load over minutes to hours. Fast-start = synchronized and at full load in about ten minutes or less.

facets.label: LCOE
facets.tip: Unsubsidized levelized cost of electricity for a new build at a reasonable site, in $/MWh. Anchored on Lazard's June 2025 US ranges where they exist (utility solar $38–78, onshore wind $37–86, geothermal $66–109, combined-cycle gas $48–109, coal $71–173, nuclear $141–220, gas peaking $149–251) and on project data elsewhere. LCOE ignores when the power arrives, so read it next to the dispatch tag.

facets.label: Cap. factor
facets.tip: Share of the year the plant delivers its rated output, at a good site in a typical market. US 2025 fleet averages: utility solar 24%, wind 34%, coal 49%, combined-cycle gas 58%, nuclear 91%. A low band is not always a weakness, since peakers are built to run 5–15% of the year.

facets.label: Capex
facets.tip: Overnight capital cost per kW of rated capacity for a new project, excluding interest during construction. Directional, and first-of-a-kind projects routinely land 2–3× above the band. Gas figures reflect 2026 pricing rather than the pre-2022 numbers still quoted in older models.

facets.label: Build time
facets.tip: Time from notice to proceed to commercial operation for a typical project. It excludes permitting, equipment lead time, and the interconnection queue, which now runs a US median above five years on its own. Lazard's 2025 construction assumptions: utility solar 15 months, onshore wind 18, offshore wind 24, gas 24, geothermal 36, coal 60–66, nuclear 84.
